newsitem.title: KENYA: Zaire rebel chief flies to South Africa - source.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel chief flies to South Africa - source.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila flew on Tuesday to South Africa for talks with President Nelson Mandela's government on civil war in eastern Zaire, a regional military source said.
"He (Kabila) left today for South Africa. We do not know how long he will stay. But the visit is part of consultations with the South Africans on the Zaire conflict," the source told Reuters.

The source, who closely monitors the war pitting Zaire's ragged army against rebels of Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), stressed that Kabila would not be meeting Zairean government representatives.

"He is not going to meet the Zaireans at all. This is purely between Kabila and the South Africans. Depending on the outcome, other initiatives will follow," said the source, who declined to be identified.

Kabila was accompanied by his chief aide on foreign affairs and member of the Alliance's national executive committee, Bizima Karaha. Karaha, a medical doctor, last week held talks with South Africa's Deputy President Thabo Mbeki in Cape Town.
In the eastern Zairean city of Goma, a rebel spokesman said Kabila left for a trip into the field but he declined to say where. He added the rebels remained interested in negotiations.
Kabila's departure came a day after Mandela said he and other African leaders would meet Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko on March 19 in a new attempt to end the civil war.
Mandela told reporters negotiators would deal separately with Kabila, who shunned a Cape Town peace meeting on Zaire at the weekend and says the only issue for negotiation in Mobutu's stepping down.
"Our first step is to see President Mobutu. There are initiatives to deal with Mr Kabila, but the first step is not to bring the two of them together," Mandela said.
Kabila has repeatedly told reporters that negotiations on the Zaire war should centre on Mobutu's handover of power he has held for the last 31 years in Africa's third largest country.
Mandela said he and leaders of countries around Zaire, including Kenya, Tanzania, Zambia and Congo, would meet Mobutu in Nairobi or at his jungle palace in Gbadolite, Zaire, on March 19.
The source said on Tuesday there was confusion in the heavily-fortified Zairean town of Kindu where government soldiers had gone on a looting spree as Kabila's forces approached.

"We hear there is generalised confusion in Kindu. Soldiers are looting the place because they know rebels are around the corner. Looting is very strong evidence in Zaire that soldiers are about to abandon a place," the source added.
Kindu, the capital of Maniema province is 80 km (50 miles) southwest of Kalima which the rebels captured several days ago.

The civil war started when ethnic Tutsis took up arms in October after local authorities tried to force them to leave Rwanda, their ancestral home. Zaire says they are backed by soldiers from Burundi, Rwanda and Uganda. All three deny the charge.
Rebels now hold a strip stretching at least 1,000-km (600 miles) from the war's starting point on the Rwanda border to Zaire's important southern copper-producing province of Shaba.
